passage:
In Irawati's village outside Nashik, the school's inter-house race was set for Republic Day: five kilometres along the canal road. She had never run further than the bus stop.
That night, under the kitchen bulb, she opened a fresh notebook page. “Get fit” was useless, she thought; you can't tick off “get fit”. So she wrote: Goal: run 5 km without stopping. Date: 26 January. Now: 1 km, from the temple to the second culvert.
She counted the weeks on the calendar: eleven. “If I add a little every week, just to the next marker stone, I'll get there with time to spare.”
Her friend Alka read the page over her shoulder. “Marker stones?”
“The canal has one every half kilometre. They're my plan.”
The next morning at six, Irawati ran to the second culvert, and stopped, exactly as written.

qa.q: What did Irawati write as her starting distance?
qa.a: 1 km, from the temple to the second culvert.

qa.q: Why did Irawati think "get fit" was useless?
qa.a: She felt it gave nothing to aim at or tick off, and a measurable goal made her feel more confident about getting there.

qa.q: What else could help Irawati stick to the plan on hard mornings?
qa.a: Running with Alka on some days, so someone expects her at six and the marker stones feel less lonely.

qa.q: How might Alka see the marker-stone plan?
qa.a: Alka may be amused at first, then impressed that the stones turn a big goal into small, visible steps.

grounding: Shows a teen writing a race date, a starting distance of one kilometre and a plan to add a little each week toward running five kilometres.

Rafiq had spent a month copying a fast bowler's drills from a video: a long run-up, a big leap, a warm-up of fifty jumping jacks. His back had started to ache after nets, the kind of ache that stayed till morning.
On Thursday, on the school ground in Hyderabad, he waited until the other boys had left and went up to Akash Sir, the school's cricket coach. “Sir, can you check my action? And tell me what warm-up I should really do?”
Akash Sir watched him bowl six balls, then six more from side-on. “You're copying someone much taller, whose body is fully grown. Your front foot lands across, and your back twists.” He shortened the run-up, fixed where the front foot landed, and swapped the jumping jacks for slow jogging, leg swings and shoulder circles.
The first balls felt slower. By the end of practice, his back didn't hurt at all.

qa.a: Slow jogging, leg swings and shoulder circles.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq wait until the other boys had left?
qa.a: He may have felt a little embarrassed to admit his drills weren't working, and wanted the coach's attention without an audience.

qa.a: Show it to Akash Sir first and ask whether it suits his build and age, since a coach who has watched him bowl can judge that.

qa.a: Akash Sir likely values a player who asks, and is relieved to fix the action before the back trouble gets worse.

By the end of the first week he was walking strangely down the stairs. I asked if he was okay. “Just sore. Pain means it's working,” he said, and went out again.
On day ten I heard him shout from the ground. His father helped him home, one arm over his shoulder. The doctor said it was a thigh strain, and no running for several weeks.

Every morning Vijay ran the tar road from his village to the highway turn and back, getting ready for the taluka athletics meet. By the second week, his right knee ached every time he climbed the steps of the well.
He said nothing at first. Then on Friday it hurt just walking to school, and he stopped pretending. After prayer, he went to Uday Sir, the PE teacher. “The knee hurts after the road. Should I stop?”
Uday Sir pressed around the knee, then looked at his rubber chappals. “You're running on tar in these? Cut the distance in half. Run the mud path by the sugarcane fields instead. The school has spare canvas shoes; take a pair. If it still hurts next week, we see the doctor at the health centre.”
Vijay ran the mud path the next Monday, half the old distance. The knee stayed quiet. Three weeks later he added the road back, a little at a time.

In their village near Margao, Maria used to play football on the church ground every evening for an hour and a half. With the Class Ten boards seven weeks away, her mother wanted her to stop completely.
Maria thought it through on the walk home. If I stop, I'll sit at the desk longer, but I already stare at the same page after dinner. If I play the full ninety minutes, I lose too much time. So what's in between?
She proposed it at dinner: twenty minutes, fixed, six to six-twenty, just passing drills with her cousin Sumit, then straight home to study. “It's not football against marks. It's so my head works.”
Her mother agreed to try it for two weeks.
By the end of the first week, Maria was finishing her evening maths set before nine, something she hadn't managed all month. Sumit complained that twenty minutes was too short. She didn't budge.

Dear Payal Didi,
You asked me to write when something changed, so here it is.
For six weeks my 100 m time was stuck. Every Saturday I timed myself, and every Saturday it was the same, or worse. I started dreading practice. I even thought of quitting sprints.
Then I remembered what you said at the camp: “You can't control the stopwatch. You can control what you do.” So I stopped timing myself every week. Instead I made a chart with two questions: did I turn up, and did I do the start drills and arm drills properly? Every practice, two ticks or not.
For four weeks I just collected ticks. Nineteen practices out of twenty. Last Saturday Coach timed us for the district list, and I ran faster than I ever have.
I'm keeping the chart. Thank you for the advice.
Pema

Leela, you asked how I got faster this year. I'm Gopika, and here's the boring secret: I stopped looking at my time.
Last summer my 200 m was stuck for two months. Same time, every Saturday. I'd cry in the changing room, then train harder, then run the same time again. My coach finally took the stopwatch away from me. Not joking, she put it in her bag.
She said, “For four weeks you have two goals. Come to every session. And do the drills: starts, high knees, arm swing, all properly.” So I kept a small notebook: attendance, drills, a tick for each. It felt like nothing. Like homework, not racing.
At the end of the month she timed me. I'd dropped time for the first time since spring. And the month after that, again.
So now I only look at the stopwatch once a month. The rest of the time, I look at my ticks.

“Nazia, you're sitting in the dark with your eyes shut. Are you asleep?”
“No, Farhan Bhai. I'm running tomorrow's district race.”
“From the sofa?”
“In my head. Watch.” She kept her eyes closed. “Warm-up at eight-thirty. Two easy laps, drills, strides. Then the call room, where everyone looks scary. I breathe: in for four, hold, out for six. Three times.”
“Then?”
“Blocks. On your marks. I look at my lane, not at the girl in lane five. Gun. Drive low for ten steps.”
“What if you trip at the start? Like last year?”
She nodded, eyes still shut. “I've planned that. If I stumble, I don't look back. I pump my arms, get upright and finish. One stumble doesn't decide it.”
“And the last bit?”
“Last thirty metres, when my legs burn, I think tall and loose, not faster. Then the tape.”
She opened her eyes. “That's twelve times I've run it this week.”

qa.q: What breathing pattern does Nazia use in the call room?
qa.a: In for four, hold, out for six, three times.

qa.q: Why has Nazia planned what to do if she stumbles?
qa.a: She is still anxious after tripping last year, and planning it in advance helps her feel calmer and ready.

qa.q: What else could Nazia rehearse besides the race itself?
qa.a: A long delay or a false start, so an unexpected wait in the call room doesn't shake her.

qa.q: How might Farhan Bhai see his sister's rehearsal?
qa.a: Farhan Bhai starts by teasing, then seems impressed by how carefully she has planned, even for last year's stumble.

The night before the district meet last year, I couldn't sleep, so I raced in my head instead. I'm Lakshmi, and I'd run the 400 m for two seasons without ever finishing well; the nerves ate me alive in the call room.
My teammate Zainab had taught me this. I lay on the hostel bed and walked through everything slowly: the warm-up jog on the back field, the drills, lacing my spikes twice. Then the stagger, the gun, the first bend, running tall on the back straight.
I planned the bad bits too. If someone drifts close, I hold my lane and keep my arms going. If I stumble, I get up and finish; one stumble doesn't decide a race. And in the call room: breathe in for four, out for six, until my shoulders drop.
Next morning my shoulders dropped on the third breath. I finished second. Zainab screamed louder than my coach.

qa.q: What place did Lakshmi finish?
qa.a: Second.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel in the call room before learning this?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt so nervous there that the nerves "ate me alive", spoiling two seasons of races.

qa.q: What else could Lakshmi add to the rehearsal next season?
qa.a: Practising the breathing during real training, not only in bed, so it becomes automatic under pressure.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel seeing Lakshmi finish second?
qa.a: Zainab is thrilled and proud, since the technique Zainab taught helped, which is why the scream was so loud.

grounding: Shows an athlete mentally rehearsing the warm-up, start and race, planning what to do after a stumble, and using a set breathing pattern to steady the nerves.
